decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files were checked and are absent for this work. In the Theoretical Background (pp. 226-227, RQ3 and RQ5), Results (pp. 239-240, Table 7), and Discussion (p. 246), the authors empirically retest Seibt & Forster's (2004) published findings that negative stereotype activation increases cautious/analytical processing (tested via the Cognitive Reflection Test and mediation analysis) and that explicit versus implicit priming induces stereotype disconfirmation, concluding that their results failed to corroborate these claims. The identity is verified in the reference list (p. 251) and Crossref metadata (DOI 10.1037/0022-3514.87.1.38, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2004). The sole shipped row (input_row_index 2431) is Carr & Steele (2010, DOI 10.1177/0956797610384146, Psychological Science), a distinct work by different authors testing ego depletion and financial decision making, so report equivalence does not apply and Seibt & Forster (2004) is a genuine omission.

In the Theoretical Background (p. 227, RQ4), the authors state that '[f]ollowing the study by Spencer et al. (1999), we first investigated whether activation of negative stereotypes increases anxiety among threatened individuals and whether state anxiety could be reliably pinned as a mediator of the effect,' test this using state anxiety (STAIshort) in the mediation model in Results (pp. 239-240, Table 7), and explicitly report in the Discussion (p. 246) that '[u]nlike previous studies (Seibt & Forster, 2004; Spencer, Steele, & Quinn, 1999), we were also unable to corroborate the mediating effect of state anxiety and analytical reasoning on behaviour under stereotype threat.' The original identity is verified in the reference list (p. 251) and Crossref metadata (DOI 10.1006/jesp.1998.1373, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 1999). Although C. M. Steele is a co-author on the sole shipped row (input_row_index 2431, Carr & Steele, 2010, DOI 10.1177/0956797610384146), Spencer et al. (1999) is an independent earlier study on women's math performance and state anxiety mediation rather than an alternate report of Carr & Steele (2010), and it is not duplicated by any other target.

In the Theoretical Background (p. 228), Results (Table 2 correlation matrix on p. 233 and Step 1 regressions in Table 8 on p. 241), and Discussion (p. 246), the authors empirically retest the published finding of Lemaster & Strough (2014) that higher self-evaluated masculinity predicts greater financial risk tolerance (lower risk aversion) regardless of biological sex, concluding: 'However, we did not corroborate this effect... masculinity was unrelated to any of the measures.' The bibliographic identity is confirmed in the reference list (p. 250) and Crossref metadata (DOI 10.1016/j.joep.2013.11.001, Journal of Economic Psychology, 2014). It is completely distinct from the sole shipped row (input_row_index 2431, Carr & Steele, 2010, DOI 10.1177/0956797610384146) and is an independent study from sibling target 4 (Meier-Pesti & Penz, 2008), so report equivalence does not apply.

decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files were checked and are absent for this work. In the Introduction (p. 223), Theoretical Background (p. 228), Results (Table 2 on p. 233 and Step 1 regressions in Tables 8-9 on pp. 241-243), and Discussion (p. 246), the authors measure masculinity and femininity with the Bem Sex Role Inventory and financial risk attitudes (including Waerneryd's 1996 scale used by Meier-Pesti & Penz, 2008) to empirically test Meier-Pesti & Penz's (2008) finding that masculinity predicts lower financial risk aversion while femininity is unrelated to risk preferences, explicitly concluding: 'However, we did not corroborate this effect. Although our results show that biological sex is not predictive of risk aversion, unlike previous studies, we found that femininity alone weakly correlated with one of the risk aversion measures, while masculinity was unrelated to any of the measures.' The bibliographic identity is confirmed in the reference list (p. 250) and Crossref metadata (DOI 10.1016/j.joep.2007.05.002, Journal of Economic Psychology, 2008). It is absent from the sole shipped row (input_row_index 2431, Carr & Steele, 2010, DOI 10.1177/0956797610384146) and is an independent primary study distinct from sibling target 3 (Lemaster & Strough, 2014).

decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files were checked and are absent for this work. Crosetto & Filippin (2016, DOI 10.1007/s10683-015-9457-9) is not mentioned anywhere in the Introduction, Theoretical Background, Hypotheses/Research Questions, Methods, or Results, and none of the four experimental risk elicitation methods appraised by Crosetto & Filippin (2016) are retested here (the present study uses Dohmen et al., 2012, Waerneryd, 1996, and Porcelli & Delgado, 2009 adapted from shipped row input_row_index 2431, Carr & Steele, 2010). In the Discussion (p. 245), Crosetto & Filippin (2016) is cited solely as general background literature showing that different risk elicitation measures often diverge, motivating an exploratory look at inter-measure correlations among the study's three REMs. Under the codebook, general methodological motivation or literature alignment without retesting a specific original finding is not a replication target.

Csermely & Rabas (2016, DOI 10.1007/s11166-016-9247-6) is never mentioned in the Introduction, Theoretical Background, Hypotheses/Research Questions, Methods, or Results, and its findings on time consistency and predictive power of multiple price list risk elicitation methods are not empirically retested. It is cited only in the Discussion as background context for gender differences in risk measures (p. 242) and for general measure inconsistency/difficulty of paired lotteries (p. 245) when discussing the three REMs used to extend the replication of shipped row input_row_index 2431 (Carr & Steele, 2010). Per the codebook, a work cited for background context or methodological comparison is not a replication target.
